20025-pirate-gold:
F. J. Stimson published Pirate Gold in 1895, a novel built around money held by an old bank. The bank had taken a national charter in 1863, during the Civil War. Yet some gold sat on no account and in no reserve. That odd gap sits at the heart of the tale.

Stimson writes about bankers, clerks, and the paper money of a new national system. Greenbacks, specie, and old habits of trade all shape the plot. Readers get a story of finance told from inside the counting room, not from a textbook.
20417-the-outline-of-science-vol-1-of-4-:
The Outline of Science, first published in 1922, set out to explain modern science to general readers. This is the first of four volumes. Its makers called the plain reader the man in the street, and wrote for him in simple, direct language.

The book offers what its preface calls a bunch of keys for locked doors. Behind those doors lie the treasures of knowledge about the heavens, the earth, and living things. Diagrams and clear chapters break hard ideas into steps. The set became a well-known doorway into science for readers with no training.
20453-the-christmas-child:
The Christmas Child is a Christmas story set on a poor farm by the sea. The land is hard to work. In every field, rocks pierce through the thin soil and stand out, grey and sharp, amid the grass and the ripening corn.

Salt-laden winds beat the farm, and money is scarce. Against that hard setting, the tale sets the season's hope and the coming of a child. Stories of this kind were written to be read aloud at Christmas. They found their warmth in simple homes, where kindness had to cover what wealth could not.
20817-the-mother-and-her-child:
No calling stands higher, says The Mother and Her Child, than that of a healthy mother. Business wives, farm wives, and wives of wealth all share one deep instinct. That claim frames a guide to pregnancy, birth, and infant care.

Doctors Lena and William Sadler wrote plain health books for American homes. This one treats feeding, illness, growth, and daily care in clear terms. It aimed to cut infant deaths with sound, calm advice. Readers today can see both the good sense and the firm moral tone that marked home health guides of the early twentieth century.
20834-ruth-fielding-at-the-war-front-or-:
No passer-by could miss Ruth Fielding, with her cheerful eye and humorous lip. At the War Front sends Ruth to France in 1918 to hunt a lost soldier. Alice B. Emerson's heroine had grown from school tales to war service by this volume.

Ruth works near the lines, facing peril with pluck and good sense. The lost soldier hunt gives the plot its pull and its heart. Girls' series books joined the war effort in their own way, with heroines who served bravely. This entry shows Ruth at her most grown-up, in khaki days far from her schoolgirl start.
21627-gambler-s-world:
Retief of the Corps Diplomatique checks his vermilion cutaway in Keith Laumer's Gambler's World, from Worlds of If in 1961. Four sets of lapels mark his rank as First Secretary and Consul. Magnan calls him to the ambassador's briefing before the Potentate enters.

On Petreac, the Nenni hold authority, and their traditions must be observed. Retief's mocking air, Magnan warns, has already delayed his rise. The trade talks have been scripted for two months, yet Retief treats them as a gamble. Laumer's Retief tales mix diplomacy, poker faces, and sly humour in a brisk space-age key.
21730-erling-the-bold:
Vikings row out from a Norwegian fiord on a bright summer morning at the start of this Ballantyne tale of old Norway. Two boats head for the same rocky islet but keep apart, their crews wary of each other. The men wear ring mail and steel headpieces, armed as men had to be in those days.

Erling, the bold hero of the title, leads the story through feuds, voyages, and fights. Ballantyne loved the northern seas, and he fills the tale with ships, storms, and the hard code of the Norsemen. It is his take on the saga world: proud men, sharp swords, and honor held dearer than life itself.
22093-the-sagas-of-olaf-tryggvason-and-o:
Two Norse kings share this volume of sagas in English dress. Olaf Tryggvason forced Norway toward Christianity at the end of the tenth century. Harald the Tyrant, better known as Harald Hardrada, was the last great Viking king. He fell at Stamford Bridge in 1066, weeks before Hastings changed England for good.

The Olaf chapters show a queen hiding by night as winter closes in. Enemies hunt her party through a frightened countryside. Battles, conversions, and sudden deaths fill both sagas, told in the spare saga style. These translations brought the kings' lives from the Icelandic histories to English readers who knew Norway mainly through its Vikings.
22593-the-shadow-world:
Hamlin Garland wrote The Shadow World, a 1908 book about psychical research and the puzzle of hypnotism and spirit claims. Garland, a well-known American novelist of farm life, turned late in his career to the study of mediums and mental phenomena. Here he reports talks and sittings with a skeptical, watchful eye.

In the sample scene, a man named Miller answers slowly. He believes in Vienna, though he has never seen it. Yet he doubts a Vienna doctor who claims he can hypnotize a patient into smiling through an amputation. That blend of faith and doubt runs through the book. Garland tests wonders against plain reason, case by case. Readers curious about the era's seance culture get a thoughtful, firsthand tour.
22938-the-camp-fire-girls-in-the-outside:
Margaret Vandercook sends her heroines beyond camp in The Camp Fire Girls in the Outside World, published in 1914. One scene turns on small, telling action. Entering the drawing room, a girl places candles on the mantelpiece. Her breath clouds faintly in the cold room. Her gown, mist-gray and clinging, suits the wintry light around her.

The Camp Fire Girls series followed its troop from woods and campfires into school, work, and the wider world promised by the title. Vandercook wrote for the new century's organized girlhood, mixing adventure with ideals of service and self-reliance. This volume's outside world tests camp lessons against city life. Period charm and period assumptions travel together through every chapter.
22974-the-city-bride-1696-or-the-merry-c:
Verse fireworks open The City Bride, a comedy of 1696 subtitled The Merry Cuckold. Pray aloud to this audience, one wit warns, and you merely oblige them, canonizing a crowd with no religion at all. Praying to such saints, he adds, can hardly count as superstition. The rhymes snap like a fan.

Restoration comedy lived on cuckolds, citizens, and sharp wives, and a city bride was its favorite engine. Money marries up, wit marries down, and everyone schemes in couplets and quick prose. Plays of this date mixed song, dance, and insult in roughly equal shares. The text preserves a minor but lively specimen, useful to anyone tracing how London laughed at marriage and trade at the century's end.
23022-red-rose-and-tiger-lily-or-in-a-wi:
Mrs. L. T. Meade introduces Hester Thornton in Red Rose and Tiger Lily, subtitled In a Wider World. Hester leaves the Grange drawing room and walks a short stretch of its wide gravel sweep, listening hard. She was about seventeen, slender for her age, with dark eyes, strongly marked brows, and abundant lighter brown hair coiled round her well-shaped head.

Meade wrote dozens of girls' novels, and Hester's step into a wider world follows her proven path. School friendships widen into society, with its tests of loyalty and love. The Grange's gravel sweep is the threshold. Beyond it wait the wider world's pleasures and snares. The book offers period girls' fiction at full polish, earnest, romantic, and sure of its moral ground.
23063-the-lost-child:
Sunlight does magic in The Lost Child, a tale dated 1894. Overnight sleet powdered every bare branch along the boulevard Malesherbes, outside the Godefroy mansion. The great magician sun, the narrator says, amused himself by turning those branches into great bouquets of red coral.

Paris sparkles first, then darkens, as a child goes missing inside the fine neighborhood. The contrast carries the story, beauty on the street, fear in the house. Tales of lost children were a period staple because they joined every reader's worst worry to a city's glitter. This one dresses the worry in lovely prose, and its boulevard opening remains its most quoted passage.
23140-the-death-shot-a-story-retold:
A modern editor confesses in The Death Shot, a story retold. The editor likes to think Reid would approve. Their version, he claims flatly, beats the published book, though some errors survive in it anyway. It makes a very nice audiobook, he adds, taking almost fifteen hours to read. He has heard it twice, and enjoyed it thoroughly.

That odd frame belongs to a retold version of Mayne Reid's frontier romance of love, jealousy, and a deadly rifle shot on the prairie. The retelling's presence raises its own questions about texts and tinkering, which the preface answers with disarming cheer. Readers get a long western of the old school, plus a small modern mystery about who improved it and why.
23150-the-albert-gate-mystery-being-furt:
Reginald Brett rests between cases in The Albert Gate Mystery, published in 1904. Work has been scarce since the celebrated case of Lady Delia Lyle's vanishing and death. Only a hard worker, Brett reflects, truly enjoys healthy idleness. A letter arrives as he dresses, inviting him to a quiet country shoot.

Louis Tracy's gentleman detective, Brett, takes further adventures here, as the subtitle promises, and a country shoot is exactly where mysteries find such men. Albert Gate, in Knightsbridge, gives the case its London address and its social shine. Tracy wrote brisk, romantic detection for readers who liked their sleuths well dressed and well connected. Idleness ends, as it must, with the first shot out of place.
a-domestic-problem-work-and-culture-in-t: Reformer Abby Morton Diaz tackles the great Victorian question: how should a household be run? Work, servants, children, and culture all come under her sensible, progressive eye. Written with warmth and common sense, the book shows one thoughtful woman's plan for making home life both efficient and humane.

desert-gold: A Western adventure novel set in the harsh deserts of the Arizona border country. doctor-marigold: Dickens's 1865 Christmas tale told by a cheap-jack, a roadside peddler, who takes in a deaf girl no one wants. Warm and stagey, it was a star turn in his public readings, and crowds wept at it. Late Dickens playing straight for the heart.

govdocs-archive_org-alistTheManWhoMisrul:
Emanuel M. Josephson, a New York physician and pamphleteer, wrote Rockefeller Internationalist: The Man Who Misrules the World as an attack on the Rockefeller family's power. He had earlier written The Strange Death of Franklin D. Roosevelt, and he dedicated this book to the Constitution.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In 1971 a top Air Force official addressed the Joint Chiefs of Staff on the arithmetic of nuclear war. William Burr edited this briefing book around his shocking sentence. America could lose two hundred million people, the official said, and still have more than it had at the time of the Civil War.

Evidence here gives the quote, year, and editor, and little more. The quote alone explains the posting. Green jade-enamel lines the windowless, doorless room throughout. Three books, The Advent, The Encounter, and The Victory, structure it. Templeton seldom left his commodious underground house anymore. Board of Health enamel and classical frieze gratings ventilate it.
marmion-a-tale-of-flodden-field:
Marmion is Sir Walter Scott's tale of Flodden Field, in Cassell's 1888 library edition. An introduction tells how the poem was begun in November 1806. Constable offered a thousand guineas for it unseen. Miller and Murray eagerly joined the venture.

Scott's first romance, The Lay of the Last Minstrel, had triumphed in 1805. Now he took more than usual pains, and enjoyed the writing. His hero Marmion is a splendid, false-hearted knight. The tale runs through castles and convents to Flodden's battlefield. There, in 1513, Scotland's king and flowers fell together. Marmion's speed and color made Scott the age's favorite poet. Its best lines are quoted still.
masters-of-the-guild:
Louise Lamprey wrote Masters of the Guild, printed in New York in 1920. Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis drew the pictures. Lamprey had told guild tales before, in In the Days of the Guild.

Peirol of the Pigeons leads, with a tale of Bellerophon tucked inside. A tournament in the clouds and a set of puppet players follow. Padraig of the scriptorium copies books in his tale. A tapestry chamber and a castle tale round out the old world scenes. To Dorothy heads the contents, as a gift note to a child. Guild crafts, music, and art give each tale its bright core.
matthew-arnold: George Saintsbury wrote Matthew Arnold for the Modern English Writers set. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The copy here is a third impression, marked with the year 1902. Saintsbury held the chair of rhetoric and English letters at Edinburgh. The hosted sample preserves only the title page and the series list. No readable chapter text appears in it, so this note stays with those front page facts.
melody-the-story-of-a-child:
Laura E. Richards wrote Melody: The Story of a Child in 1894. She gave the book to the memory of her sister. Julia Romana Anagnos is named in that tender dedication.

Eleven chapters trace the child from The Child to Light. The Doctor, On the Road, and Rosin the Beau come early. A churchyard, a serpent, and a lost child darken the middle. Waiting and Blondel lead toward the last two heads, Darkness and Light. A line from Sidney Lanier heads the contents page. Child grief and child hope shape the short arc of the tale.
miss-mcdonald:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes built this novel largely out of journals and letters. The contents open with extracts from Frances Thornton's journal, then Guy's, then Daisy's. An author's story interrupts the diaries, followed by a chapter called The Divorce. Five years later, the tale resumes with Daisy's letter and a visit to Saratoga.

Holmes was a bestselling author of domestic novels like Millbank and Ethelyn's Mistake. Here she lets three diarists tell one tangled story from three sides. A sick-room scene and the late chapter named Miss McDonald bring the threads together. The form suits her readers, who liked confession, courtship, and consequence.
my-days-and-nights-on-the-battle-field:
Charles Carleton Coffin wrote this Civil War book for young readers. Dana Estes issued it in Boston, copyrighted in 1887. Coffin had written Boys of '76 and Following the Flag. The book opens with a note to the youth of the United States.

Chapter one asks how the Rebellion came about. Coffin had reported the war from the field himself. His title promises days and nights spent on battlefields. He tells of marches, fights, and the men who bore them. The book taught a new generation the war their fathers fought, in plain words meant to stir memory and pride.
nasa-tm-19660007963-models-of-the-earth-:
Joseph C Cain at Goddard presented these models of Earth's magnetic field in Bergen, Norway, on August 16, 1965, and dated the paper October 1. A field model is a formula that gives the field's strength and direction anywhere. Cain builds the core field model from magnetometer data gathered on land and at sea, per the catalog note.

Good models serve navigation, geology, and spacecraft work alike. They also reveal slow changes in the deep field over time. Cain spoke at an institute on radiation trapped in the field. That link is practical: trapped particle paths are traced through the very field his models describe for other users.
nasa-tm-19660010209-recent-measurement-o:
J P Heppner reported recent satellite measurements of the magnetic field far from Earth in this Goddard paper. The data came from the EGO-1 satellite, also called OGO-A in the catalog note. The outer magnetosphere and its boundary regions are the areas covered. There, Earth's field is stretched and pressed by the solar wind, and its shape was still being mapped.

Field readings from a satellite in that region test every model. The boundary moves with solar conditions, so single readings can mislead. Heppner gathers recent results into one report for other workers. Such compilations let the next team plan orbits and instruments with the newest map of near-Earth space in hand.
nasa-tm-19670009023-earth-s-magnetic-fie:
Harold L. Stolov, of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York, wrote this survey of Earth's magnetic field. It opens with the compass needle, the simplest proof of the field, and with William Gilbert, who first grasped the field's global character. Gilbert's 1600 treatise argued, from experiments with a spherical lodestone, that Earth itself is a great magnet.

About ninety percent of the main field, Stolov notes, matches a short dipole at Earth's center. The dipole tilts about eleven and a half degrees from the rotation axis. The survey recalls the first measurements of compass deviation in the sixteenth century and the first world charts of declination. The catalog record lists the wider topics covered: the dipole field, the magnetosphere, quiet-day geomagnetic variations, and dynamo theory for the ionosphere's origin.
nasa-tm-19680010616-theoretical-study-of:
Y. C. Whang, of the Laboratory for Space Sciences at Goddard Space Flight Center, models the Moon's shadow in space in January 1968. The solar wind cannot pass through the Moon, so a long, quiet wake trails behind it. Inside that wake, the magnetic field bends in ways worth predicting.

Whang builds a model for the field's disturbances in the plasma shadow. He solves Maxwell's equations directly for steady solutions. The disturbance is blamed on three kinds of drift currents in the plasma. His computed field changes match what the Explorer 35 satellite actually saw. The agreement backs the model's picture of the wake.
nasa-tm-19690028319-an-analysis-of-the-d:
Winifred Sawtell Cameron and George J. Coyle, of Goddard Space Flight Center, analyze boulder distribution near small lunar craters in this August 1969 preprint. Impacts scatter rocks inside and around the craters they blast out. A casual impression said the patterns differ by crater type. The pair set out to test that impression with statistics instead of eyeballing.

They inspected Lunar Orbiter III photographs from three lunar regions with a magnifying lens. Six hundred three craters wider than about a hundred meters entered the survey. Each crater's boulders were classed as spread far out, held within the crater and its rim, or not visible at all. The sites included ground near the Ranger and Surveyor landing zones.
now-it-can-be-told:
Philip Gibbs named his war book Now It Can Be Told, and its preface explains the title. Parts cover observers and commanders, the school of courage, and the nature of a battle. A winter of discontent, the heart of a city, and psychology on the Somme follow. The fields of Armageddon and for what men died close the plan.

Gibbs writes of aspects of the war the world must know and remember, he says. The book stands as a memorial of men's courage in tragic years. It also warns that war will happen again if evil and folly stay in peoples' hearts. He claims his daily reports from the western front stood truthful and accurate.
old-love-stories-retold:
Richard Le Gallienne retold famous love stories in prose. The hosted text holds one story from the book. That story treats poet Heinrich Heine and his Mathilda. The Gutenberg note says only this chapter is present. It warns readers that the file is partial.

His graceful hand gives the tales a tender tone. Readers of the hosted text get the Heine story alone. They should not expect the full printed collection here. Even alone, the piece shows his literary style. The file came out in June 2002 as text 3267. Volunteers typed it for free reading by all, it says.
prose-idylls-new-and-old: Charles Kingsley gathers prose idylls — short, lovely pieces on nature, country life, and the sea, old and new. His muscular Christian warmth colors every page. Gentle, manly writing from a beloved Victorian parson. Short, sunlit pieces on woods, waters, and country folk, old favorites and new, glow with his hearty faith.
reginald: Saki’s Reginald drawls through dull tea parties, skewering bores. The keenest wit of his age, in stories and quips. Small bright blades on every page. Wit that has never lost its edge, on every page.
round-the-world: Before he became the world's richest man, steel magnate Andrew Carnegie took a grand tour of the globe — and wrote this lively memoir of the journey. From London to India to Japan, he reports on the people, railways, and wonders he met with a businessman's curiosity. The book shows a young industrialist discovering the wider world he would soon help reshape.
sailing-alone-around-the-world: Between 1895 and 1898, retired sea captain Joshua Slocum did what no one had ever done: he sailed around the world alone. His little sloop Spray carried him 46,000 miles through storms, pirates, and long lonely weeks at sea. Written with dry humor and a sailor's eye for weather and waves, this true story remains the classic account of single-handed voyaging.
sienkiewicz-so-runs-the-world:
Shorter fiction by Sienkiewicz fills So Runs the World, here in English. Tales and sketches of modern Poland sit beside character studies and brief parables. The Nobel laureate works here on a smaller scale than in his vast historical epics.

Village folk, gentry, and dreamers pass through these pages in turn. Some tales cut with satire, while others rest in quiet pathos. His famed ease of telling never flags, even in a few pages. Readers who know Quo Vadis will find a fine companion here, proof that his range reached well beyond the epic canvas.
sir-francis-drake-s-famous-voyage-round-: Francis Pretty's account of Drake's famous voyage round the world: the 1577-1580 circumnavigation. The Elizabethan epic, firsthand. The sea dog's great voyage. The 1577 voyage, firsthand, elizabethan epic, Elizabethan epic, the sea dog's great voyage, firsthand, the sea dog's great voyage, told firsthand.
sketches-new-and-old: Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old: the early humor collected. Jumping frogs and blue jays. The young humorist's best. A comic treasury, jumping frogs and blue jays collected, young Twain's comic best, a treasury of humor.
ten-days-that-shook-the-world: John Reed's 1919 Ten Days That Shook the World: the Russian Revolution eyewitnessed. The great American reportage, passionate and vivid. History's most famous dispatch. Reed saw the Revolution from inside, his dispatch is history on fire, the classic of witness.
the-christmas-child: The Christmas Child, by Hesba Stretton. The holiday tale. This book preserves that story. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
the-crock-of-gold: James Stephens's 1912 Irish fantasy: the philosopher, his wife, and leprechauns with a crock of gold mix philosophy with fairy mischief. Whimsical, witty, and deeply Irish, it is a unique delight. The Irish imagination at its most playful.
the-education-of-the-child: Ellen Key's 1900 manifesto for the "century of the child," arguing that education should follow nature, not crush it. The Swedish reformer's call for kindergartens, free play, and respect for children's individuality influenced progressive schooling worldwide. Idealistic and humane, it helped change how the modern world raises its young.
the-golden-threshold: Poems by Sarojini Naidu, the Indian poet and freedom fighter called the Nightingale of India. Written in English with Indian music in every line, they sing of love, springtime, temples, and the beauty of her homeland. Published in 1905, the collection introduced Western readers to a new voice, lyrical and proud, from a nation awakening.
the-home-and-the-world: Rabindranath Tagore's great novel sets a Bengali woman between her devoted husband and a charismatic nationalist leader. Home and world, tradition and change, pull at her heart. The Nobel laureate's most searching work of fiction, profound and moving. Torn between love and cause, his heroine embodies a nation's painful awakening.
the-ivory-child: H. Rider Haggard's 1916 Ivory Child: an African idol and its guardian. Exotic adventure in his late manner. Vintage Haggard, an idol's guardian guards Haggard's secret, african mystery, African mystery in Haggard's late manner, exotic adventure in late manner.
the-junior-classics-volume-5-stories-tha: William Patten's Junior Classics were designed to put the world's best stories into children's hands, and this fifth volume collects tales meant to be loved for a lifetime. Fairy tales, fables, and adventure stories appear in versions trimmed for young readers. Generations of families read these volumes aloud together, making the series one of the most cherished children's libraries of the early 1900s.
the-life-and-death-of-cormac-the-skald: This saga tells Cormac the skald's Viking life and verse. Swords sang. The Tower library holds the full text. It skalds old. Battles raged. Verses lived. North remembered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-master-of-the-world: Jules Verne's Master of the World brings back the sinister Robur. His terrible new machine defies every army on earth. Strock the detective hunts the sky pirate without rest. A thrilling scientific romance, told by Verne at full speed.
the-story-of-a-child: French novelist Pierre Loti recalls his own childhood in this lyrical memoir — a sensitive boy growing up in a quiet seaside town, dreaming of distant lands. His earliest impressions of nature, family, and the sea unfold in prose of great beauty. The book reveals the roots of the wanderlust that would fill his famous travel novels.
the-two-guardians-or-home-in-this-world: The Two Guardians, or Home in This World, by Charlotte Yonge. The orphans' tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
the-vicar-of-wakefield: Oliver Goldsmith's 1766 Vicar of Wakefield: Dr. Primrose's family, their trials, and their goodness. The most beloved English novel of the 18th century, tender and comic. A timeless classic. Goldsmith's good vicar endures all with a smile, the most lovable novel of the 18th century.
the-way-of-the-world: William Congreve's 1700 masterpiece, the greatest comedy of the Restoration stage. Mirabell and Millamant duel through the famous "proviso" scene, bargaining over the terms of their marriage with unmatched wit. Every line sparkles; the plot is a clockwork marvel. The summit of English comic drama.
the-winds-of-the-world: The Winds of the World, Talbot Mundy's novel of India in the Great War. Its tale unfolds. This book preserves that adventure. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
the-wood-beyond-the-world:
William Morris wrote this tale of a quest in a made up world in 1894. Many call it the first modern fantasy set in a world made whole from the mind. Morris had made his own line of prose romance, in a high style of his own.

Golden Walter flees a bad marriage by sea and is cast on a strange shore past the world's rim. A wood of wonders, a cruel maid, and a kind one mark his road home and to love. The book founds the line of tales set in a second world, made new from whole cloth.
this-simian-world: Clarence Day — beloved humorist of Life with Father — looks at human society through the eyes of apes in this witty satire. Our customs, wars, and follies appear delightfully absurd from the simian point of view. Clever, humane, and quietly subversive.
to-have-and-to-hold: Mary Johnston's 1900 To Have and to Hold: a Virginia romance of Jamestown. The bestseller that made her famous, gallant and thrilling. Colonial America in love. Jamestown's perils frame a gallant love, the colonial romance supreme.
un-doc-declaration-of-the-rights-of-the-:
The Declaration of the Rights of the Child was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly on 20 November 1959. It builds on a 1924 Geneva text of the same name. Children need special care before and after birth, the preamble says. Mankind owes the child the best it has to give.

Ten short principles carry the message. Each child holds every right here, with no bar of birth or creed. The child's best interests rule when laws are made. A child gets a name and a nationality from birth. Food, housing, health care, and free basic schooling are all promised. So are play, love, and first call on relief. No child may be trafficked, neglected, or put to harmful work.
what-s-wrong-with-the-world: G. K. Chesterton's 1910 book of essays diagnosing modern ills: big business, big government, and the loss of the home. Witty, paradoxical, and passionately argued, it defends the small and the local. Chesterton the prophet at full power.
